clue.text: Psychiatrist's contract

definitions.meaning: slang from 'headshrinker', a joking name for a psychiatrist
the verb: to get smaller, not a legal document

explanation.surface: A psychiatrist's employment contract.
explanation.walkthrough: The ’s stands for 'is', joining the two meanings. 'Contract' looks like a noun, a legal document, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for a psychiatrist comes from 'headshrinker'; as a verb it is a plain synonym for contract, to get smaller.

clue.text: Large crowd he's taken round old road

indicators.note: HE is wrapped round the other letters, holding them inside

parts.note: taken as written; the outer letters
O is the standard abbreviation for old
RD is the abbreviation for road

explanation.surface: A man who has led a large crowd along an old road.
explanation.walkthrough: The ’s is short for 'has': he has taken round, so the pronoun splits to go either side of the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a horde is a large, often unruly, crowd.

clue.text: Giving full details of home department hotel

parts.note: DEPT is the abbreviation for department
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A report detailing the Home Department's hotel bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Home department' reads as one government office, like the Home Office (the UK ministry for domestic affairs), but it splits in two.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: an account done in depth covers the subject thoroughly, leaving no detail out.

clue.text: Sportswear set for assembly

definitions.meaning: British word for a team's playing strip
a box of parts to be put together, as for a model

explanation.surface: Sports clothing laid out ready for a school assembly.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage a sports team's uniform is its kit; 'assembly' is not a school gathering but putting parts together.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses of one word: the clothing and equipment for a sport, and a packaged set of parts to build something.

clue.text: Site contains a magnificent residence

explanation.surface: A building site that includes a grand house.
explanation.walkthrough: The single letter goes in straight after the first letter of the site.
explanation.definitionFit: A palace is the official home of a monarch or bishop, the model of a grand residence.

clue.text: Act almost had to go through

indicators.note: the word is not quite complete: its last letter goes

parts.note: act = PERFORM, minus its last letter

explanation.surface: A law that was nearly obliged to be passed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Act' looks like legislation, and 'go through' like a bill passing; in fact act means perform and go through means pierce.
explanation.definitionFit: To perforate is to pierce with holes, so to go right through a surface.

clue.text: Clear openings for lawbreakers upset detectives

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letters of lawbreakers and upset
CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, British police detectives

explanation.surface: Obvious chances for criminals have annoyed the detectives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' looks like a reversal instruction but is just one of the two words supplying first letters. CID is the plain-clothes branch of British police.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: lucid writing or thinking is clear and easy to follow.

clue.text: Brave guy in bed for a smoke

parts.note: a cot is a small bed
a hero is a brave man

explanation.surface: A bold man lying in bed with a cigarette.
explanation.walkthrough: The brave guy goes after the first letter of the bed, not at its start.
explanation.definitionFit: A cheroot is a cigar with both ends cut square, so 'a smoke' in the everyday sense of something smoked.

clue.text: Extremely clever reviser of text, to whom I'm indebted

indicators.note: take the extremes, the two end letters

explanation.surface: Praise for a brilliant editor to whom the writer owes a debt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely clever' reads as high praise, but extremely asks for the outer letters. The definition is a descriptive phrase for the person owed money.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the creditor is the person a debt is owed to, seen from the debtor's side.

clue.text: Prepare to swallow cold cut

parts.note: C is the standard abbreviation for cold, as on taps
to hew is to cut, as with an axe

explanation.surface: Getting ready to eat a slice of cold meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cold cut' reads as a slice of meat; it splits into two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: chewing breaks food down so it can be swallowed.

clue.text: Turn on waterworks with very little pressure

parts.note: P is the symbol for pressure

explanation.surface: Opening the water mains when the pressure is very low.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn on the waterworks' is an idiom for starting to cry, dressed up here as a plumbing job.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: to turn on the waterworks is to start crying, often for effect.

clue.text: Little flower in cold fall

definitions.meaning: a small white bulb that flowers in late winter
read literally: a fall of the cold white stuff

explanation.surface: A small flower seen during a cold autumn.
explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning is playful: 'fall' reads as autumn, but a fall of snow is a snow drop, split into its two parts.
explanation.definitionFit: The snowdrop is a small white flower of late winter; the second sense is cryptic, a literal drop of snow.

clue.text: Perhaps Oscar Wilde caught at last, breaking law

indicators.note: take the last letter of each word

parts.note: the last letters of Wilde and caught

explanation.surface: Oscar Wilde, finally arrested for breaking the law.
explanation.walkthrough: Oscar Wilde really was jailed, which makes the surface convincing; the name splits, Oscar joining 'Perhaps' as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: an Oscar, the Academy Award, is one kind of statuette, which 'Perhaps' signals.

clue.text: A maths broadcast is source of inspiring problems

indicators.note: letters scattered, as seed is broadcast

explanation.surface: A televised maths lesson that sets students puzzling problems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inspiring' is used literally: breathing in. 'Maths' is the British word for math.
explanation.definitionFit: Asthma causes difficulty breathing in, problems with inspiring in its literal sense.

clue.text: Mobility device firm put in store for renovation

indicators.note: STORE is renovated, its letters rearranged

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company

explanation.surface: A company brings a mobility scooter into a shop being refitted.
explanation.walkthrough: The firm sits after the first letter of the rearranged shop.
explanation.definitionFit: A mobility scooter is a small motorised vehicle for people who have trouble walking.

clue.text: Divides up bulbs for cooking (not the first two)

explanation.surface: Splitting onions for a recipe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bulbs' suggests flowers or light bulbs; 'for cooking' pins it to the onion family.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to allot is to share out portions, dividing something up among people.

clue.text: Caught one without protective coat

indicators.note: caught as in heard, caught what someone said

explanation.surface: Someone arrested without a coat on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught' looks like C, the cricket abbreviation, but it means heard. The one without is a made-up word, a person who lacks.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacquer is a hard varnish brushed on to seal and protect a surface.

clue.text: Messy room used for lengthy sleeper

indicators.note: the letters are in a mess, jumbled

explanation.surface: An untidy bedroom where someone sleeps for hours.
explanation.walkthrough: The sleeper is an animal, not a person or a railway carriage.
explanation.definitionFit: The dormouse hibernates for months, and is proverbially sleepy, as at the Mad Hatter's tea party.

clue.text: Person in charge is frantically busy

parts.note: IC = in charge, as in 2IC, second in command

explanation.surface: The boss is run off their feet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Person in charge' looks like one phrase for a boss; it is two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal sense: a manic day or person is wildly, frantically active.

clue.text: Cloak and headgear, last of range

indicators.note: the 'last of' a word is the letter that ends it, so only the final letter of range is used

explanation.surface: The final items in a clothing range: a cloak and a hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cloak and headgear' reads as a list of clothes; only cloak is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a cape is a short sleeveless cloak.

clue.text: Iron the newspapers

definitions.meaning: the verb: to smooth clothes with a hot iron
collective name for journalism, from the printing machine

explanation.surface: An instruction to iron out the creases in the papers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Iron' could be the metal, but here it is the household verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Two plain senses: pressing clothes smooths them as ironing does, and the press is the collective name for newspapers.

clue.text: Heads turned in shock

explanation.surface: People turning their heads in surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heads turned' reads as people looking around; nut is slang for head, as in 'use your nut'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a blow or piece of news can stun, leaving someone dazed with shock.

clue.text: Partly shaved heads of thugs on news somehow upset residents every day

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.words: thugs on news somehow upset residents every day

explanation.surface: Skinhead thugs in the news are upsetting the locals daily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' looks like an anagram signal, but every word after 'heads of' just supplies its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Tonsure is the monk's shaved crown with a ring of hair left around it, so the head is only partly shaved.

clue.text: Small bite and small drink

definitions.meaning: a little pinch with the teeth

explanation.surface: A snack and a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Both meanings are nouns; the clue's appeal is how ordinary it looks.
explanation.definitionFit: Two noun senses of one word: a quick pinching bite, and a small measure of spirits.

clue.text: Old, unusually clear prophecy

indicators.note: the letters are arranged in an unusual way

parts.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: An ancient prediction that was, for once, unambiguous.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a joke about oracles, famous for riddling answers.
explanation.definitionFit: The word can mean the prophetic pronouncement itself, not only the one who makes it.

clue.text: Study American country's energy

parts.note: the possessive S, taken as written
E is the symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Researching a nation's energy policy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'American' suggests the USA, but the country is in South America.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the verb means to read through carefully, to study in detail.
